name: six photographs named by their framing, not their subject
one_line: Six rows, none of which names anything to photograph: each names a property the picture itself has to have.
how: Write six rows describing the picture and never the subject: one in which the size of the thing cannot be told, one where the important thing is off centre, one of a spot already photographed in another of the six but from a different height, one showing that somebody was there and has gone, one that cannot be understood. Say the subject is anything within reach. Give one shot each and print that: one shot is what puts the weight back on deciding, and it is the setting to fix. Add a narrow column for how many framings were discarded before the one taken. Then two questions to be answered while looking at the six together: in which did you discard most, and in which is there something you had not seen while shooting.

knobs.knob: naming the subject or the framing
knobs.effect: A subject makes the photograph a receipt and only works where the writer knows the place. A framing makes the photograph the answer, works in a house nobody has seen, and two people shooting the same thing hand back two different answers.
One makes the choice cost something and is the reason the discard column has anything in it. Many turn the task into selection afterwards, which is easier, later, and a different activity.
The count is a number for the only part of the work a finished picture does not keep. It costs one narrow column, has no wrong answer, and is most of what the sheet gets back besides the images.

knobs.knob: whether the person has to be in the frame
knobs.effect: Without, it documents a thing. With, it documents having been there, and the form turns from a hunt into proof of presence — a different afternoon, worth choosing rather than drifting into.

where_the_work_is: In the six rows naming a property of the image. They are the only part written in advance, and they are what makes each answer a decision rather than an errand.
breaks: None of the six can be checked. Whether the first really hides the scale, whether the fifth really shows an absence — nobody can say, including whoever wrote the rows. A photograph is evidence that something was done and never that it was done well. What comes back is six images and a sheet of small numbers; on 800x480 the six rows fit as text and no photograph does.
